newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy hard-left lashes Scalfaro on welfare.
newsitem.headline: Italy hard-left lashes Scalfaro on welfare.

text.p: Italy's main hard-left party stepped up its opposition to social spending cuts on Tuesday with an attack on President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro after he joined calls for a prompt reform of the welfare state.
Fausto Bertinotti, whose hard-left Communist Refoundation party is an uneasy ally of Prime Minister Romano Prodi, told La Stampa that it was the government's job to decide policy.
"If (Scalfaro) has something very important to say to the country, he should write a message to parliament," he said.
"We can talk about the welfare state but not starting from the pre-conceived idea that we have to make cuts," he added.
Scalfaro, who is on an official trip to Germany, unexpectedly entered Italy's thorniest political row after talks in Berlin on Monday with German Preisdent Roman Herzog.
He said structural reforms were necessary and that the welfare system "should be reformed systematically, right now."

Italy spends less overall than many of its European Union partners on welfare, but economists say its bloated pensions system must be tackled to make sure Rome is fiscally fit enough to qualify for the launch of Europe's single currency.

Bertinotti's warnings came as the government braced itself for a report by the European Commission, due to be published on Wednesday, which one EU source has said will show Italy lagging on a key deficit target for economic and monetary union (EMU).

The source said it would forecast that Italy's 1997 deficit will be 3.2 percent of gross domestic product -- above the three percent limit set by the Maastricht Treaty. EMU entrants will be chosen next May on the basis of their 1997 economic performance.

Italy says it is making great strides on the deficit and already meets other key criteria, including inflation, which preliminary data published on Monday suggested would be 1.8 percent in March, its lowest level since May 1967.
Prodi has staked his political life on taking Italy into EMU at its scheduled launch in 1999. But Bertinotti is unrelenting on social spending and says welfare may prove his downfall.
Prodi's centre-left government almost collapsed earlier this month when Refoundation, whose support is needed for a majority in parliament, refused to back a security mission for Albania.
Bertinotti told La Stampa that the government should "cement itself" on the question of welfare and that it was right for it to fall if it could not find a common idea.
Cabinet undersecretary Enrico Micheli welcomed Scalfaro's intervention in a radio interview and said welfare should be tackled "immediately."

Responding to Bertinotti, he added: "If a (ruling alliance) cannot stay together it is obvious that it will fall and we would need to seek other formulae because what is clear is that this country cannot miss the extraordinary goal of entering into Europe."
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said no-one wanted to cut current pension levels but welfare would be addressed in the government's three-year economic plan (DPEF), due by mid-May.
"We will have to talk about it," Ciampi told Corriere della Sera. "The DPEF will indicate the lines the government intends to follow which will then be elaborated in budgetary measures."
Left-leaning daily La Repubblica called the welfare state "a national emergency".
"We've beaten inflation, we're beating the public sector deficit, now we have to settle up the welfare state," it said.
It added: "There's no point kidding ourselves. Until there is thorough welfare reform, we will never be a normal country."
